 The Bobby Brink Experiment Isn't Paying Dividends
 The Bobby Brink Experiment Isn't Paying Dividends 
 Image courtesy of Sergei Belski-Imagn Images
 By 
 Eric Forga 
 - Saturday at 11:10 AM 
 The Minnesota Wild did not trade for Bobby Brink because of his feel-good homecoming story . They needed a forward who could strengthen their offense and make their lineup more dangerous. However, the return hasn't generated much excitement. The experiment looks like a bust, even if there is still time for Brink to change that assessment.  
 Minnesota acquired the Minnetonka native from Philadelphia on March 6, sending defenseman David Jiricek the other way. Brink arrived with 13 goals and 26 points in 55 games that season, plus 41 points the previous year.  
 There was a legitimate hockey argument for taking a chance on him. He wasn’t simply a player with a Minnesota birth certificate and nothing else to offer. Still, a reasonable argument for a trade is different from the results afterward. 
 Brink finished the 2025-26 regular season with two goals and four points in 13 appearances for Minnesota. Through his first 11 games this season, he has five assists but no goals. He has contributed, but it’s hardly the offensive impact that would make the Wild feel confident they found an answer.  
 His goal drought is particularly frustrating because Minnesota needs more than occasional flashes from its supporting forwards. Brink doesn’t have to become a superstar. However, he needs to give opponents another player to worry about instead of leaving the heavy lifting to the team’s biggest offensive threats.  
 There are mitigating circumstances. An upper-body injury interrupted his initial stretch with Minnesota, and his average ice time this season has hovered around 13 minutes. It would be unfair to judge him as though he's had unlimited opportunities in a premium offensive role.  
 Still, opportunity and production work both ways. Players need minutes to establish themselves, but they also need to produce enough to earn more responsibility. Brink’s lack of production can’t be about opportunity indefinitely. Five assists deserve acknowledgment. So does the impressive pass he made on October 12 to set up Danila Yurov against Vegas.  
 Those moments show the ability. The problem is turning individual highlights into dependable impact.  
 The Wild likely didn’t give up a future star in Jiricek. Still, the Wild exchanged an asset for Brink, and that decision should be judged by what Brink actually provides, not by whether the player going the other way struggles.  
 The standard should be straightforward: Does he improve the lineup? Does he create offense consistently? Can the coaching staff trust him with a meaningful role?  
 Right now, the production isn't there to call this trade a success. There’s time to change that, but patience should come with expectations, not excuses. That brings up the broader point: The Wild should never confuse a local connection with a roster-building advantage.  
 No evidence suggests Guerin acquired Brink solely because he is from Minnetonka. His previous NHL production offered a clear reason to pursue him. But the principle still matters: Being from Minnesota should be a nice detail, not a deciding factor.  
 Fans want a championship contender, not a reunion of familiar hometown names. Every acquisition should face the same evaluation: talent, fit, cost, upside, and expected contribution. Brink can still make this work. But he needs to start finishing chances and producing consistently.  
 The homecoming story has already been told. Now he needs to give Minnesota a hockey reason to celebrate.

 mnfaninnc

 Posted Saturday at 12:38 PM 
 My eye test sees that Brink has not really found chemistry with anyone. In fact, he seems to get in the way a lot. I don't know why this is, does he just not read the game the way we play it? 
 Now, as for the scoring, does he do the other little things needed to stay in the lineup? Does he throw his body around with hits? Does he block shots and create turnovers? His assist to Hartman was also really good. He's made some plays at the blue line. He's not one to go nail someone in the boards, but he also is competitive in board battles. His puck bobbling drives me nuts. 
 I'd like to see what happens after he gets 1 goal, if floodgates open for him. I do wonder if he is trying too hard. Typically, players who do this end up out of position and that could explain the "getting in the way." Brink's got some interesting offensive instincts, but I'm not sure of the fit. 
 My conclusion is don't give up on him, but should you need kap space on a trade, including him is getting more favorable. I do like seeing him shooting more.

 In the few years I've been watching hockey more than simple entertainment eye, I've understood that hockey teams seem to go thru cycles, like 10 years of economy condensed into 41(42) home games and 41(42) away games.  Especially the Minnesota Wild.  I've seen how we have bull runs and depressions all inside a season.  2026-27... show me where this time, this season, is normal or consistent.  Where is our starting goalie?  How about our other star blue liner?  Where is the 1C that was intended to solidify our attacking lines, provide more secondary / depth scoring?  Each game has been shuffling lines based on who's available, and composition of who we play against.  I will give the pessimists the nod that many Wild players are managing the shuffle very well.  However, I'll wait to pass Brink judgement until our roster is closer to normal and Brink can find stability to find his groove.  Some are late bloomers, but if he's given multiple chances and shows no improvement or extra effort to improve, then let's have that talk.
